---
order: 1
unit: warmup
title: One main idea, one extra
summary: "A main clause makes sense on its own. A dependent clause adds something to it, such as when, why or if, and cannot stand alone. A joining word (a subordinating conjunction) such as because, until, if or after links them. Putting the two together makes a complex sentence that says more than two short ones."
language: maths
node: [AC9E4LA06 n1, AC9E4LA06 n2, AC9E4LA06 n3]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Ava kept swimming can stand alone, so it is the main clause. Although the water was cold cannot, so it is the dependent clause. Although adds a surprise to the main idea." }
hook: "'If you want to win.' Is that a whole sentence?"
---
A **clause** is a group of words built around a verb. There are two kinds:

- A **main clause** makes sense on its own. It can be a whole sentence.
- A **dependent clause** adds extra information (when, why, if) and cannot stand alone. It starts with a **joining word** (also called a subordinating conjunction) such as *because*, *until*, *if*, *after* or *while*.

A sentence with a main clause and a dependent clause is a **complex sentence**.

## Predict: which part can stand alone?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Predicting which half of a sentence can stand alone shows students they already feel the difference between a complete idea and an add-on."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "'When the bell rang, the students lined up.' Which part could be a whole sentence on its own?"
  options: ["When the bell rang", "the students lined up", "Both parts", "Neither part"]
  actual: "'The students lined up' stands alone. 'When the bell rang' leaves you waiting to hear what happened, so it is the add-on, the dependent clause."
```

## Try: main or dependent?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Labelling both halves of four sentences shows that the joining word belongs to the dependent clause and that the order of the halves can change."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 470 }
hint: ["Click a part, then choose Main clause or Dependent clause.", "Ask of each part: could it be a whole sentence on its own?"]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "'after the game ended' is part of a sentence. Could it be a whole sentence on its own?", options: ["No, it leaves you waiting to hear what happened", "Yes, because it has a verb", "Yes, because it starts with a joining word"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Having a verb isn't enough. It also needs to be a complete idea.", "A joining word makes a part depend on another, so it works against standing alone."], explain: "It leaves you waiting for more, so it is a dependent clause." }
check: { type: board, text: "Label each part of each sentence as a main clause or a dependent clause.", when: "n_right = 8 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "Because it was raining, If the creek rises, until the bus arrived and while she washed the dishes cannot stand alone, so they are dependent clauses. The match was cancelled, the class waited, the track will close and Mia sang each stand alone. The dependent clause can come first or last." }
```

Were you right about the bell? 'The students lined up' stood alone, and 'when the bell rang' was the extra.

## Worked example: what does the extra add?

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Matching joining words to what they add, catching a dependent clause pretending to be a sentence, and choosing the one that gives a reason shows the clause is chosen for the meaning it adds."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each joining word to what its clause adds."
      pairs:
        - ["after", "When: time"]
        - ["because", "Why: reason"]
        - ["unless", "What must be true: condition"]
        - ["as if", "How: manner"]
      explain: "The joining word tells the reader how the extra idea connects to the main one: when it happens, why, what has to be true, or how."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is Nib's recount, one sentence per line. One line is only a dependent clause, so it cannot stand alone. Click it."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: clause-alone
      explain: "Line 3: 'Because the water was high.' leaves you waiting for what happened. Nib needs a main clause: 'Because the water was high, Ms Okafor told us to stay back.'"
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which sentence tells you why the group packed up?"
      options: ["We packed up because the storm was coming.", "We packed up before the storm arrived.", "We will pack up if the storm arrives.", "We packed up when the storm arrived."]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Before tells you when, not why.", "If tells you what has to be true.", "When tells you the time."]
      explain: "Because gives the reason. The joining word decides what kind of extra information the dependent clause adds."
```

### Three steps for any complex sentence

```worked
\text{Find the joining word} :: Look for because, until, if, after, while, although.
\text{Test each part} :: Could this part be a whole sentence on its own?
\text{Name what it adds} :: When? Why? What must be true? How?
```

Now match the joining words.

### Find the clause that cannot stand alone

### Which one gives the reason?

## Vary: choose the joining word

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Choosing the joining word that fits each sentence shows the word decides the meaning the dependent clause adds."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 330 }
hint: ["Read each sentence with each choice. Only one makes sense.", "Read each sentence aloud with each choice, and ask which one says what you mean."]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the joining word that fits each sentence.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "Because gives the reason the match was cancelled, until says how long we wait, and as if says how Mia ran. The wrong choices make nonsense, which shows the joining word is doing real work." }
```

## Practise: find the joining words

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Colouring the joining words in a short text shows where each dependent clause starts."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 300 }
hint: ["Choose Chain 1, then click each word that joins a dependent clause to its main clause.", "Each one starts the extra part of its sentence."]
check: { type: board, text: "Colour the three joining words.", when: "chains_ok = 1 and n_stray = 0", explain: "After, while and If each start a dependent clause. They link the extra idea to the main one." }
```

## Make: a recount with extras

In your own document, write at least three sentences of a recount, such as a school excursion or a day out. Use at least two different joining words, such as *when*, *because*, *after*, *until* or *while*.

Here is one example: "On Tuesday our class visited the wetlands. We wore boots **because** the ground was muddy. **After** we ate lunch, we counted the birds."

Then swap with a partner. Point to each dependent clause and say what it adds: when, why, what must be true or how. Could it stand alone?

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing three sentences of a recount with two different joining words puts complex sentences to work in a real text type."
hint: ["Think of a school excursion or a day out. Write what happened.", "Use at least two different joining words, such as when, because, after, until or while."]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote a recount with at least two joining words, and a partner and I checked that no dependent clause is left on its own as a sentence." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that a sentence can have a main clause, which stands
  alone, and a dependent clause, which adds when, why, if or how and cannot.
  They label both halves of four sentences, match joining words to what they
  add, catch a dependent clause left as a sentence, choose the joining word that
  fits, colour joining words, and write three sentences of a recount.
time: 45
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 5 min · Practise 5
  min · Make and own writing 15 min
goals:
  - I can tell a main clause from a dependent clause.
  - I can name the joining word and what it adds (when, why, what must be true,
    how).
  - I can spot a dependent clause left on its own as a sentence.
  - I can write a recount that uses complex sentences.
struggle: Students label by position (the first part is the main clause) or by
  length. Ask 'could this part be a whole sentence on its own?' and let them
  test each part aloud.
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: four sentences, two kinds of clause.


  The one idea: a main clause stands alone and a dependent clause adds to it.
  This lesson covers AC9E4LA06 nodes 1 to 3 (independent and dependent clauses,
  subordinating conjunctions and the relationships they create, and writing
  complex sentences). ACARA says **independent clause**; the lesson says **main
  clause**, and names the term once so you can search for it. A **subordinating
  conjunction** appears as a **joining word**.


  The board labels what is planted. The Make step has no board: students write
  the recount in their own document, and a partner or you decide whether each
  dependent clause really cannot stand alone.


  All the sentences are made up for the lesson. Dependent clauses are not the
  same as sentence fragments the student writes by accident, but the bug task
  shows how a dependent clause on its own becomes one.
running:
  - "Predict: ask what the class would expect to hear next after 'When the bell
    rang,'."
  - "Try: after labelling, ask which part could be moved to the other end of its
    sentence. (All four can.)"
  - "Worked example: Nib's recount. Ask what a reader wants to know after
    'Because the water was high.'"
  - "Vary: ask students to say what the wrong choices would mean, to hear why
    they make nonsense."
  - "Make: partners point to each dependent clause and test whether it could
    stand alone."
stuck:
  - see: A student labels 'the match was cancelled' as dependent because it comes
      second.
    ask: Could 'the match was cancelled' be a whole sentence on its own?
    fix: "Test by position-free question: can it stand alone? The order can change,
      so the test is the only reliable one."
  - see: A student leaves the joining word out of the dependent clause.
    ask: Is 'it was raining' the whole extra part, or does 'because' belong to it
      too?
    fix: The joining word starts the dependent clause and is part of it.
  - see: A student's Make recount has a dependent clause as a sentence on its own.
    ask: Read it aloud. Do you want to hear what happens next?
    fix: Join it to a main clause, with a comma if it comes first.
stretch: "Take one main clause (the class visited the wetlands) and write four
  sentences that add a different kind of dependent clause: when, why, what must
  be true, how. Which gives the most useful information to a reader?"
support: "A sentence card: a box for the main clause, a box for the extra, and a
  list of joining words."
leads: >
  Next in Building sentences: how to say what people said, and how the order of
  clauses changes what a reader notices.


  Complex sentences are the base for embedded clauses (Detail inside a sentence)
  and compound-complex sentences (Shaping sentences).
exit:
  q: "'We stayed inside until the storm passed.' Which part is the dependent
    clause, and what does it add?"
  a: "'Until the storm passed' is the dependent clause. It adds a time: how long
    they stayed inside."
explain: >
  A **clause** is a group of words built around a verb.


  - A **main clause** makes sense on its own.

  - A **dependent clause** adds extra information and cannot stand alone. It
  starts with a **joining word**: because, until, if, after, while.


  Ask of any part: could this be a whole sentence on its own? If not, it depends
  on another clause. The joining word tells the reader what the extra part adds:
  when, why, what must be true, or how.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Why do writers use dependent clauses instead of lots of short sentences?
    prompts:
      - Say 'The match was cancelled. The oval was flooded.' Now say it with
        because. What does the joining word do that the full stop did not?
      - Which version would you rather read in a long recount?
    notes: The joining word tells the reader how the two ideas connect. Two short
      sentences leave the reader to work that out. A complex sentence says it,
      and a long text reads more smoothly.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Stand-alone test
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Read out parts of sentences from a class novel or textbook. Students
        stand if the part could be a whole sentence on its own and sit if it
        could not.
      notes: Choose parts that begin with a joining word and parts that don't.
        Stand-up and sit-down makes the test physical.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Point to the extra
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Partners read each other's recounts and point to every dependent clause.
        The writer says what it adds: when, why, what must be true or how.
      notes: If a partner can't find the joining word, the writer may have used two
        short sentences. Ask whether a joining word would help.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Main or dependent?
      type: question
      q: "'While the kettle boiled, Ava found two mugs.' Which part is the dependent
        clause?"
      options:
        - While the kettle boiled
        - Ava found two mugs
        - Neither
      answer: 0
      explain: While starts a part that adds a time and cannot stand alone. Ava found
        two mugs could be a whole sentence.
```

s dependent: until the bus arrived.
para:
s dependent: If the creek rises,

widget: cohesion

mode: chain
